title: Effects of light on human circadian rhythms, sleep and mood
review_question: This article reviews our current state of knowledge regarding the effects of light on circadian rhythms, sleep, and mood.

synthesis_conclusions: Light is the most important zeitgeber for the human circadian system, influencing rhythms, sleep, and mood.
Nocturnal artificial light can disrupt circadian rhythms and sleep.

Light therapy is an effective, non-invasive treatment for various psychiatric conditions (SAD, non-seasonal depression, bipolar depression, gender-related mood disorders) and other medical conditions (anorexia, bulimia, dementia, ADHD, sleep-wake disorders in geriatric care, renal/cirrhotic patients, brain injury, Parkinson's).
The timing and regularity of light exposure are critical for its therapeutic effects, with early morning light being most pronounced for antidepressant effects.
The retina, particularly ipRGCs, mediates the non-visual effects of light, but rods and cones also contribute.
Adverse reactions to light therapy are generally rare and manageable by adjusting timing or dosage.
evidence_gaps: The exact relationship between the availability of artificial light and circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders (CRSWD) remains to be established.
Many aspects of the effects of light on the circadian clock are still largely unknown.
Teasing apart how different retinal elements contribute to the effects of light on circadian rhythms, sleep, and mood remains an important challenge.
The long-term adaptive influences of the 'spectral diet' in the real world remain an important area of investigation.
It is unclear whether the same negative results (e.g., from prolonged e-reader use) can be expected for shorter light exposures.
How much of the reported detrimental effect of smartphone use on sleep is due to light per se, or to some other feature (e.g., psychological engagement), is currently not known.

The precise mechanisms by which light exerts a positive influence on mood are currently not known, and the applicability of animal model findings (retina-habenula pathway) to humans needs more research.
Implementing dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) assessment in clinical practice remains difficult due to limited availability of equipped centers and costs.

moderators.effect: Determines the direction of circadian phase shift (morning light advances, evening/night light delays) and influences the antidepressant effect (most pronounced in early morning).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Morning light advances clock, evening/night light delays clock. Early morning light most pronounced for antidepressant effect.

moderators.variable: Photic history (amount of light seen during the day)
moderators.effect: Modulates both melatonin suppression and circadian phase shifts.
Influences the magnitude of effects on sleep and circadian rhythms (e.g., prolonged e-reader use showed significant effects, shorter exposures may not).
Bright light therapy is particularly effective when exposure occurs regularly (e.g., daily for 30-60 min).

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light, particularly short-wavelength (blue) light, is detected by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) and transmitted via the retinohypothalamic tract to the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN), thereby regulating circadian rhythms, sleep, and mood.

mechanism_chain.description: Light exposure activates specific retinal photoreceptors, leading to signals transmitted to the SCN, which then regulates circadian rhythms and downstream physiological and psychological effects.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
Regulation of circadian rhythms (e.g., melatonin suppression, phase shifting)
Effects on sleep, mood, and cognitive performance

environmental_features: light spectrum (e.g., blue-enriched light, red light)
timing of light exposure (e.g., morning, evening)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: variable, ranging from minutes to continuous exposure over days
control_conditions: different light spectra (e.g., red light as a control for blue light)
